claim: Motor coordination is supported by an array of highly organized heterogeneous modules in the cerebellum.
source: Motor coordination is supported by an array of highly organized heterogeneous modules in the cerebellum.
evidence: This is a general statement about cerebellar organization supported by established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: Transgenic mice expressing GFP in specific subsets of Purkinje cells were used to target a given set of cerebellar modules.
source: In this study, we used transgenic mice expressing GFP in specific subsets of Purkinje cells that allowed us to target a given set of cerebellar modules.
evidence: This describes the experimental methodology used in the study.

claim: Stereotyped patterns of functional synaptic organization exist between the granule cell layer and Purkinje cells, Golgi cells and molecular layer interneurons.
source: Combining in vitro recordings and photostimulation, we identified stereotyped patterns of functional synaptic organization between the granule cell layer and its main targets, the Purkinje cells, Golgi cells and molecular layer interneurons.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study based on experimental data from in vitro recordings and photostimulation.

claim: Each type of connection displayed position-specific patterns of granule cell synaptic inputs that do not strictly match with anatomical boundaries.
source: Each type of connection displayed position-specific patterns of granule cell synaptic inputs that do not strictly match with anatomical boundaries but connect distant cortical modules.
evidence: This is a primary finding based on experimental observations of connectivity patterns.

claim: The connectivity patterns connect distant cortical modules.
source: Each type of connection displayed position-specific patterns of granule cell synaptic inputs that do not strictly match with anatomical boundaries but connect distant cortical modules.
evidence: This is a primary finding based on experimental data showing long-range connectivity.

claim: The connectivity patterns can be adjusted by activity-dependent processes.
source: Although these patterns can be adjusted by activity-dependent processes, they were found to be consistent and predictable between animals.
evidence: This is based on experimental data showing plasticity effects on connectivity patterns.

claim: The connectivity patterns were found to be consistent and predictable between animals.
source: Although these patterns can be adjusted by activity-dependent processes, they were found to be consistent and predictable between animals.
evidence: This is a primary finding based on comparison of connectivity patterns across multiple animals.

claim: Long-range connectivity between brain areas and the basic organization of microcircuits has been widely studied in many brain structures.
source: Long-range connectivity between brain areas and the basic organization of microcircuits has been widely studied in many brain structures (Shepherd and Grillner, 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The synaptic connectivity at the mesoscale level has been described in few brain areas since module boundaries are often ill defined.
source: However, the synaptic connectivity at the mesoscale level, that is, the precise functional synaptic arrangement between cortical modules, has been described in few brain areas since module boundaries are often ill defined.
evidence: This is a general statement about the state of the field supported by established knowledge.

claim: In the rodent barrel cortex and visual cortex, anatomical modules contain a wide array of neuronal types that interconnect within complex neuronal circuits.
source: In the rodent barrel cortex and visual cortex (Callaway and Katz, 1993; Briggs and Callaway, 2001; Shepherd et al., 2003), anatomical modules contain a wide array of neuronal types that interconnect within complex neuronal circuits (Harris and Mrsic-Flogel, 2013; Cossell et al., 2015)
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: Inter-modular communication might influence the output of individual modules in cortical systems.
source: and reveal inter-modular communication that might influence the output of individual modules (e.g. see multi-whisker stimuli; Estebanez et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature and involves speculative reasoning about functional implications.

claim: In the cerebellar cortex, anatomical modules are well defined and are associated with different features of motor control.
source: In the cerebellar cortex, where anatomical modules are well defined and are associated with different features of motor control
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about cerebellar organization.

claim: The crystalline structure of the cerebellar cortex initially led to the concept that different functions arose through distinct patterns of input/output connectivity.
source: the crystalline structure of the cortex initially led to the concept that different functions arose through distinct patterns of input/output connectivity as observed in the barrel cortex with a given vibrissa targeting one specific barrel (Ito, 1984).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Cerebellar modules consist of an array of microcircuits, each of which has a specific identity.
source: However, much anatomical and functional evidence suggests that cerebellar modules consist of an array of microcircuits, each of which has a specific identity (Scott, 1963; Lange et al., 1982; Brochu et al., 1990; Dehnes et al., 1998; Mateos et al., 2000; Wadiche and Jahr, 2005; Sarna et al., 2006; Shin et al., 2009; Kim et al., 2009; Xiao et al., 2014; Zhou et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: Cerebellar modules are defined by the topographical organization of climbing fiber inputs to Purkinje cells and PC to cerebellar nuclei connections.
source: Cerebellar modules are defined by the topographical organization of climbing fiber (CF) inputs to Purkinje cells (PCs), originating in the inferior olive, and PC to cerebellar nuclei connections.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about cerebellar anatomy and organization.

claim: Olivo-cortical and cortico-nuclear projections delimit parasagittal zones and subzones of the cerebellar cortex called 'microzones' having similar CF receptive fields.
source: Olivo-cortical and cortico-nuclear projections delimit parasagittal zones and subzones of the cerebellar cortex called 'microzones' having similar CF receptive fields (Oscarsson, 1979; Voogd and Glickstein, 1998; Sugihara and Shinoda, 2004; Voogd and Ruigrok, 2004; Buisseret-Delmas and Angaut, 1993; De Zeeuw et al., 2011; Voogd, 1967).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: A microzone corresponds to the cortical element of a cerebellar module.
source: Thus, a microzone corresponds to the cortical element of a cerebellar module.
evidence: This is an inference based on the anatomical organization described in previous statements.

claim: PCs from a given microzone receive and integrate information from specific parts of the body and project to restricted areas of the cerebellar nuclei.
source: PCs from a given microzone receive and integrate information from specific parts of the body and project to restricted areas of the cerebellar nuclei, which in turn send the cerebellar computation to the cerebral cortex, brainstem or spinal cord (Voogd and Glickstein, 1998).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The complete olivo-cortico-nuclear loop defines the cerebellar module.
source: The complete olivo-cortico-nuclear loop defines the cerebellar module (Figure 1A; Figure 1—figure supplement 1; for review see Ruigrok, 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation and reference to figures.

claim: Mossy fiber inputs partially overlap with the receptive fields of CFs when originating from the same body part.
source: Mossy fiber (MF) inputs, the second major excitatory pathway of the cerebellum, partially overlap with the receptive fields of CFs when originating from the same body part (Garwicz et al., 1998; Pijpers et al., 2006; Voogd et al., 2003).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: The cerebellar cortex is subdivided into individual microzones each controlling a given set of muscles.
source: Therefore, it has been suggested that the cerebellar cortex is subdivided into individual microzones each controlling a given set of muscles (Apps and Garwicz, 2005; Thach et al., 1992).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations and involves inference about functional organization.

claim: Some boundaries between different microzones can be identified by a family of neurochemical markers, the zebrins, selectively expressed in PCs.
source: Some boundaries between different microzones can be identified by a family of neurochemical markers, the zebrins, selectively expressed in PCs (Figure 1—figure supplement 1) (Apps and Hawkes, 2009; Brochu et al., 1990).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations and reference to a figure.

claim: The level of expression of zebrin markers has been associated with specific synaptic properties and intracellular transduction pathways at the parallel fiber-PC or CF-PC synapses.
source: The level of expression of some of these markers has been associated with specific synaptic properties and intracellular transduction pathways at the parallel fiber (PF)-PC or CF-PC synapses (Wadiche and Jahr, 2005; Paukert et al., 2010; Cerminara et al., 2015; Hawkes, 2014)
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: Different intrinsic properties of PCs and different rules for plasticity induction exist between zebrin positive and negative bands.
source: leading to the description of different intrinsic properties of PCs and different rules for plasticity induction between zebrin positive and negative bands.
evidence: This is an inference based on the association between zebrin expression and synaptic properties mentioned in the previous statement.

claim: The cerebellar cortex is composed of an ensemble of heterogeneous modules.
source: Combined with the regional differences in the cytoarchitecture of the cerebellar cortex (for review see Cerminara et al., 2015), these findings demonstrate that the cerebellar cortex is composed of an ensemble of heterogeneous modules.
evidence: This is an inference based on the evidence of zebrin expression patterns and regional differences cited.

claim: Cell identity relies on its position in the cerebellar cortex.
source: Therefore, an appealing hypothesis would be that cell identity relies on its position in the cerebellar cortex and that specific communication rules between neighboring microzones might arise from this anatomical and neurochemical heterogeneity.
evidence: This is presented as a hypothesis based on the heterogeneity described.

claim: Specific communication rules between neighboring microzones might arise from anatomical and neurochemical heterogeneity.
source: Therefore, an appealing hypothesis would be that cell identity relies on its position in the cerebellar cortex and that specific communication rules between neighboring microzones might arise from this anatomical and neurochemical heterogeneity.
evidence: This is presented as a hypothesis to be tested.

claim: Granule cells relay the MF input within the cerebellar cortex.
source: Intermodular communication might involve granule cells (GCs), which relay the MF input within the cerebellar cortex.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about cerebellar circuitry.

claim: GCs have long transverse axons, the PFs, that make glutamatergic synapses with hundreds of PCs across several microzones.
source: GCs have long transverse axons, the PFs, that make glutamatergic synapses with hundreds of PCs across several microzones (Harvey and Napper, 1991; Thach et al., 1992).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: PFs could define an associative pathway that enables MF inputs from one original microzone to communicate with a distant one.
source: PFs could thus define an associative pathway that enables MF inputs from one original microzone to communicate with a distant one.
evidence: This is an inference based on the anatomical organization of PFs.

claim: PCs are excited by a unique set of GCs localized in the same microzone as themselves.
source: Paradoxically, several studies have shown that PCs are excited by a unique set of GCs localized in the same microzone as themselves (Cohen and Yarom, 1998; Bower and Woolston, 1983; Brown and Bower, 2001; Isope and Barbour, 2002).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: Local GCs provide the major input to PCs.
source: These results suggest that local GCs provide the major input to PCs and that the majority of GC-PC synapses are silent (Ekerot and Jorntell, 2001; Isope and Barbour, 2002).
evidence: This is an inference based on cited studies.

claim: The majority of GC-PC synapses are silent.
source: These results suggest that local GCs provide the major input to PCs and that the majority of GC-PC synapses are silent (Ekerot and Jorntell, 2001; Isope and Barbour, 2002).
evidence: This is an inference based on cited studies.

claim: PCs can be driven by a restricted subset of GCs belonging to a different microzone.
source: In contrast, other studies demonstrated that PCs can be driven by a restricted subset of GCs belonging to a different microzone (Ekerot and Jörntell, 2003; Dean et al., 2010; Jörntell and Ekerot, 2002; Ekerot and Jorntell, 2001).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: PCs can be excited by a broad range of GCs.
source: Finally, recent studies have suggested that PCs can be excited by a broad range of GCs (Walter et al., 2009)
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Feedforward inhibition through the MF-GC-molecular interneuron pathway might play a role in the restriction of receptive fields in PCs.
source: and that feedforward inhibition through the MF-GC-molecular interneuron pathway might play a role in the restriction of receptive fields in PCs (Cramer et al., 2013; Santamaria et al., 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations and involves speculation about functional mechanisms.

claim: The wide range of functional connectivity might explain the regional differences in information processing.
source: Finally, this wide range of functional connectivity might explain the regional differences in information processing (Cramer et al., 2013) underpinned by the molecular and cellular heterogeneity between individual microzones and by the specific topographical organization of MF and CF inputs in the cerebellar cortex.
evidence: This is speculation about the functional implications of connectivity patterns.

claim: Seven putative microzones extend to the P2+ band on both sides of the midline in EAAT4-eGFP mice.
source: By comparing EAAT4-eGFP/zebrin II expression and cortico-nuclear projections, we postulated that seven putative microzones extend to the P2+ band on both sides of the midline (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison of expression patterns and anatomical projections.

claim: Bilateral MF projections were reconstructed after in vivo unilateral injection of AAV2/1-GFP viruses into the external cuneate nucleus or fluoro-ruby.
source: So that the description of the cerebellar afferents could be completed, bilateral MF projections were reconstructed after the in vivo unilateral injection of AAV2/1-GFP viruses (N = 4 animals) or fluoro-ruby (N = 2 animals) into the external cuneate nucleus
evidence: This describes the experimental methodology used.

claim: Projections from the external cuneate nucleus and lumbar spinal cord were mutually exclusive in lobules III and IV.
source: Projections from these two precerebellar nuclei were mutually exclusive in lobules III and IV, identifying an alternation of two to three parasagittal bands (mean width = 193 ± 24 µm, Figure 1C,D; n = 13 slices, N = 4 animals for cuneate projections; n = 4 slices, N = 1 animal for spinal projections) in the mediolateral axis.
evidence: This is a finding based on experimental data from viral tracing.

claim: 22% of cuneate projections were found in the contralateral vermis.
source: Notably, when measuring the GFP level of expression, 22% of cuneate projections were found in the contralateral vermis, illustrating the importance of bilateral MF inputs.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from experimental data.

claim: The comparison of the zebrin II pattern with MF inputs identified overlapping parasagittal bands.
source: Interestingly, the comparison of the zebrin II pattern with MF inputs identified overlapping parasagittal bands (Figure 1D) (Ji and Hawkes, 1994) with one shared boundary at the P2+/P2− transition.
evidence: This is a finding based on experimental data and comparison with cited literature.

claim: MF inputs subdivided the P1− band into smaller regions.
source: Also, MF inputs subdivided the P1− band into smaller regions.
evidence: This is a finding based on experimental data.

claim: CF and MF inputs delimit 13 regions having a unique combination of inputs between P2+ipsi and P2+contra.
source: Finally, CF and MF (Figure 1D) inputs delimit 13 regions having a unique combination of inputs between P2+ipsi and P2+contra.
evidence: This is a finding based on experimental data.

claim: These regions might correspond to smaller processing units than microzones.
source: These regions might therefore correspond to smaller processing units than microzones (Ozden et al., 2009; Tsutsumi et al., 2015).
evidence: This is speculation based on the anatomical findings and cited literature.

claim: Patterns of GC inputs in PCs were found to be highly heterogeneous.
source: Interestingly, patterns of GC inputs in PCs were found to be highly heterogeneous (Figure 2D), with dense local inputs (mean local charge = 10.3 ± 13.8 pC, n = 49) and silent sites, that is, no GC patch had a Z-score > 3.09 at any depth of the GC layer (38% of sites were silent; Z-score < 3.09; Materials and methods).
evidence: This is a primary finding based on experimental data from photostimulation experiments.

claim: 38% of sites were silent in GC-PC connectivity mapping.
source: Interestingly, patterns of GC inputs in PCs were found to be highly heterogeneous (Figure 2D), with dense local inputs (mean local charge = 10.3 ± 13.8 pC, n = 49) and silent sites, that is, no GC patch had a Z-score > 3.09 at any depth of the GC layer (38% of sites were silent; Z-score < 3.09; Materials and methods).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from experimental data.

claim: Remotely connected GC patches separated by silent sites were always found.
source: Remotely connected GC patches separated by silent sites were always found and were also frequently observed on contralateral sites (mean charge in distant patches = 6.1 ± 8.8 pC. Mean distance from the local peak = 215 ± 86 µm).
evidence: This is a primary finding based on experimental data.

claim: In five cells out of 49, no obvious local inputs were observed although distal inputs were present.
source: In five cells out of 49, no obvious local inputs were observed although distal inputs were present.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from experimental data.

claim: Local GCs make a strong connection with PCs most of the time, but exceptions may occur.
source: Altogether, these findings demonstrate that while local GCs make a strong connection with PCs most of the time, exceptions may occur.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing variable connectivity patterns.

claim: GCs located at several hundred micrometers from the recorded PC can make strong connections via their PFs.
source: Also, GCs located at several hundred micrometers from the recorded PC can make strong connections via their PFs, while neighboring patches can be silent, indicating that information originating in distant microzones can have a strong influence on a given PC.
evidence: This is a primary finding based on experimental data.

claim: Information originating in distant microzones can have a strong influence on a given PC.
source: Also, GCs located at several hundred micrometers from the recorded PC can make strong connections via their PFs, while neighboring patches can be silent, indicating that information originating in distant microzones can have a strong influence on a given PC.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing distant connectivity.

claim: A significant correlation was found between patterns of GC inputs for eight out of nine pairs of adjacent recorded PCs.
source: Although some strongly connected GC sites were specific to one PC of the pairs, we found a significant correlation between patterns of GC inputs for eight out of nine pairs of adjacent recorded PCs (Figure 2C; r = 0.74 ± 0.14, n = 9 pairs, N = 5 animals)
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from experimental data on paired recordings.

claim: PCs belonging to the same microzone and sharing similar MF inputs also displayed similar GC synaptic input maps.
source: indicating that in a given animal, PCs belonging to the same microzone and sharing similar MF inputs also displayed similar GC synaptic input maps.
evidence: This is an inference based on the correlation data from paired recordings.

claim: Neighboring PCs make powerful connections with a specific set of distant microzones while ignoring others.
source: These findings suggest that neighboring PCs make powerful connections with a specific set of distant microzones while ignoring others.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing selective connectivity patterns.

claim: The correlation matrix revealed four clusters of PC groups displaying a highly correlated GC connectivity map.
source: Strikingly, the correlation matrix revealed four clusters of PC groups displaying a highly correlated GC connectivity map (Figure 4A; clusters 1–4).
evidence: This is a primary finding based on computational analysis of experimental data.

claim: PCs from different animals but at the same specific location in the mediolateral axis have selected similar GC sites.
source: These results strongly argue that PCs from different animals but at the same specific location in the mediolateral axis (i.e. the vermal part of lobule III/IV) have selected similar GC sites.
evidence: This is an inference based on the correlation analysis across animals.

claim: None of the identified PC clusters clearly matches with a set of anatomical boundaries.
source: Notably, none of these clusters clearly matches with a set of anatomical boundaries as illustrated by the comparison with zebrin II bands and MF inputs from the external cuneate and the spinal cord (green rectangles, Figure 4A) indicating that boundaries of the functional organization between microzones differ from a pure anatomical description.
evidence: This is a primary finding based on comparison of functional and anatomical data.

claim: Boundaries of the functional organization between microzones differ from a pure anatomical description.
source: indicating that boundaries of the functional organization between microzones differ from a pure anatomical description.
evidence: This is an inference based on the mismatch between functional clusters and anatomical boundaries.

claim: For all PC groups, strong GC connections were always found in ipsilateral P2+.
source: However, it should be noted that for all PC groups, strong GC connections were always found in ipsilateral P2+ while a large area of the P1− band was silent.
evidence: This is a finding based on analysis of connectivity patterns across all PC groups.

claim: A large area of the P1− band was silent for all PC groups.
source: However, it should be noted that for all PC groups, strong GC connections were always found in ipsilateral P2+ while a large area of the P1− band was silent.
evidence: This is a finding based on analysis of connectivity patterns across all PC groups.

claim: The highly heterogeneous patterns of GC connectivity are stereotyped and associated with four identified clusters of PCs.
source: These findings showed that the highly heterogeneous patterns of GC connectivity are stereotyped and associated with four identified clusters of PCs, suggesting that a distinct functional organization linking distant regions might be superimposed on the anatomical microzonal framework.
evidence: This is an inference based on the cluster analysis and consistency across animals.

claim: A distinct functional organization linking distant regions might be superimposed on the anatomical microzonal framework.
source: These findings showed that the highly heterogeneous patterns of GC connectivity are stereotyped and associated with four identified clusters of PCs, suggesting that a distinct functional organization linking distant regions might be superimposed on the anatomical microzonal framework.
evidence: This is speculation about the functional implications of the findings.

claim: 81% of GC synaptic inputs to GoCs were made by local GCs.
source: Within the mapped area, we found that 81% of GC synaptic inputs to GoCs were made by local GCs as assessed by the histogram of the median Z-score (Figure 5A), for GoCs recorded in any of the four clusters of PCs identified (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from experimental data on GoC connectivity.

claim: The pattern of GC inputs to GoCs was centered on GoCs with a mean extension of 114.1 ± 70.1 µm.
source: The pattern of GC inputs was centered on GoCs with a mean extension of 114.1 ± 70.1 µm, which falls within the average range of the reconstructed GoC axonal plexus (214 ± 30 µm, n = 10; inset Figure 5A).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from experimental data.

claim: Neither the connectivity map nor the extension of the GoC axonal plexus were limited by zebrin boundaries.
source: Neither the connectivity map nor the extension of the axonal plexus were limited by zebrin boundaries (Figure 5—figure supplement 1) as opposed to GoC apical dendrites (Sillitoe et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a finding based on experimental data and comparison with cited literature.

claim: Excitatory inputs to a given GoC appear to be mostly restricted to GCs that can be targeted by the local axon of the same GoC.
source: Thus, unlike GC inputs to PCs, excitatory inputs to a given GoC appear to be mostly restricted to GCs that can be targeted by the local axon of the same GoC, confirming that they implement a local inhibitory feedback circuit in the GC layer (Cesana et al., 2013).
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data and cited literature.

claim: Some hotspots of GC inputs to MLIs did not overlap perfectly with patches of GCs that elicit strong inputs in PCs from cluster 1.
source: Strikingly, some hotspots did not overlap perfectly with patches of GCs that elicit strong inputs in PCs from cluster 1 (Figure 5B, see arrow and compare with PC from cluster 1 in Figure 4), indicating that for PCs and MLIs located in the same area, different groups of GC inputs can be selected.
evidence: This is a finding based on comparison of connectivity patterns between PCs and MLIs.

claim: For PCs and MLIs located in the same area, different groups of GC inputs can be selected.
source: indicating that for PCs and MLIs located in the same area, different groups of GC inputs can be selected.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison of connectivity patterns.

claim: GCs can relay MF information to PCs through two distinct pathways, the MF-GC-PC and MF-GC-MLI-PC pathways.
source: These findings suggest that GCs can relay MF information to PCs through two distinct pathways, the MF-GC-PC and MF-GC-MLI-PC pathways.
evidence: This is an inference based on the differential connectivity patterns observed.

claim: 86 sites (22%) displayed a significant modification in synaptic charge after plasticity induction.
source: After plasticity induction, 86 sites (22%; n = 8 cells) displayed a significant modification in synaptic charge (△Z-score > 3.09 or < −3.09; Figure 6A-figure supplement 1; Materials and methods), while no effect was observed in the remaining sites.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from plasticity experiments.

claim: The plasticity induction protocol induced postsynaptic LTP or LTD at the GC-PC synapse.
source: As already observed, this protocol induced postsynaptic LTP (green squares, Figure 6A; Coesmans et al., 2004) or LTD (blue squares, Figure 6A; Hartell, 1996) at the GC-PC synapse
evidence: This is a finding based on experimental data and cited literature.

claim: All plasticity changes were blocked by a combination of drugs that prevented the induction of plasticity.
source: All these changes were blocked by a combination of drugs that prevented the induction of plasticity (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from control experiments.

claim: A negative correlation was observed between the initial synaptic weight of the GC site and the sign of the effect after induction.
source: A negative correlation was observed (slope 0.31 and r = 0.38) between the initial synaptic weight of the GC site (high Z-score) and the sign of the effect after induction, with stronger connections leading to LTD while weaker connections undergo LTP (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from analysis of plasticity data.

claim: Stronger connections led to LTD while weaker connections underwent LTP.
source: A negative correlation was observed (slope 0.31 and r = 0.38) between the initial synaptic weight of the GC site (high Z-score) and the sign of the effect after induction, with stronger connections leading to LTD while weaker connections undergo LTP (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from analysis of plasticity data.

claim: Of the 56 sites that were potentiated, 33 were silent in the initial map.
source: Conversely, of the 56 sites (14% of total sites) that were potentiated, 33 were silent in the initial map (white 'x' in green squares in Figure 6A; Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from plasticity experiments.

claim: Previously undetectable synaptic connections were awakened by the plasticity protocol.
source: This suggests that previously undetectable synaptic connections were awakened and that the overall connectivity map can be modified by activity.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of silent sites becoming active.

claim: The overall connectivity map can be modified by activity.
source: This suggests that previously undetectable synaptic connections were awakened and that the overall connectivity map can be modified by activity.
evidence: This is an inference based on the plasticity experiments.

claim: A new distant region, initially silent, became significantly connected to the PCs belonging to cluster 1 after plasticity induction.
source: Although a few percent of the total number of PFs crossing the dendritic tree of the PCs had been stimulated, a new distant region, initially silent, became significantly connected to the PCs belonging to cluster 1, demonstrating that the connectivity map is adjustable (see * in the panel 'Difference' in Figure 6B).
evidence: This is a finding from plasticity experiments showing modification of connectivity patterns.

claim: The connectivity map is adjustable.
source: demonstrating that the connectivity map is adjustable (see * in the panel 'Difference' in Figure 6B).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the plasticity experiments.

claim: Functional microzones may communicate through the selection of GC-PC synapses in a specific set of PC clusters.
source: Therefore, functional microzones may communicate through the selection of GC-PC synapses in a specific set of PC clusters.
evidence: This is speculation about the functional implications of the plasticity findings.

claim: In all cells tested, GC inputs became detectable after the induction protocol when silent sites were specifically stimulated.
source: In all cells tested, GC inputs became detectable after the induction protocol (mean △charge from −0.4 ± 0.33 to −1.27 ± 1 pC).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from targeted plasticity experiments.

claim: Silent sites can be specifically awakened at any position in the mediolateral axis.
source: In order to assess whether silent sites can be specifically awakened at any position in the mediolateral axis, the induction protocol was reproduced by uncaging glutamate specifically on silent patches of GCs (chosen at random distances from the recorded cell) at 1 Hz for 5 min (n = 5 cells; Figure 6C).
evidence: This is a finding from targeted plasticity experiments.

claim: The functional pattern of GC inputs to PCs results from the active tuning of synapses.
source: These findings demonstrate that the functional pattern of GC inputs to PCs results from the active tuning of synapses.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the plasticity experiments.

claim: Clusters of neighboring PCs share common rules for the selection of GC inputs.
source: Our data revealed that: (1) clusters of neighboring PCs share common rules for the selection of GC inputs (Figure 7A);
evidence: This is a summary of the primary findings.

claim: PFs communicate MF information over a long distance in the cerebellar cortex linking cerebellar microzones through GC-PC and GC-MLI synapses.
source: and (2) PFs communicate MF information over a long distance in the cerebellar cortex linking cerebellar microzones through GC-PC and GC-MLI synapses while GC-GoC synapses appear mostly restricted to intra-microzonal communication (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is a summary of the primary findings.

claim: GC-GoC synapses appear mostly restricted to intra-microzonal communication.
source: and (2) PFs communicate MF information over a long distance in the cerebellar cortex linking cerebellar microzones through GC-PC and GC-MLI synapses while GC-GoC synapses appear mostly restricted to intra-microzonal communication (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is a summary of the primary findings.

claim: Spatial patterns of connectivity are predictable and consistent between animals.
source: Furthermore, we demonstrated that spatial patterns of connectivity are predictable and consistent between animals, suggesting that specific sets of cerebellar functional microzones are reproducibly combined together following similar operational rules.
evidence: This is a summary of the primary findings.

claim: Specific sets of cerebellar functional microzones are reproducibly combined together following similar operational rules.
source: Furthermore, we demonstrated that spatial patterns of connectivity are predictable and consistent between animals, suggesting that specific sets of cerebellar functional microzones are reproducibly combined together following similar operational rules.
evidence: This is an inference based on the consistency of patterns across animals.

claim: The functional synaptic organization of GC inputs to PCs and MLIs and GoCs does not strictly respect anatomical and neurochemical boundaries.
source: Finally, the functional synaptic organization of GC inputs to PCs and MLIs and GoCs does not strictly respect anatomical and neurochemical boundaries.
evidence: This is a summary of the primary findings.

claim: The preferred organization of GC inputs to PCs and MLIs suggests that microzones may have specific roles in the context of behavioral tasks associated with the anterior vermis.
source: The preferred organization of GC inputs to PCs and MLIs (in lobules III and IV of the anterior vermis) among different animals suggests that microzones may have specific roles in the context of the behavioral tasks associated with this cerebellar region, notably during adaptive locomotion (Apps and Garwicz, 2005; Dean et al., 2010).
evidence: This is speculation about the functional implications of the findings, supported by citations.

claim: Different areas of the cerebellum might have specific operational rules.
source: There are several possible explanations for this discrepancy: (1) the different areas of the cerebellum studied (i.e. the C3 zone rather than medial lobules III and IV) might have specific operational rules.
evidence: This is speculation about regional differences in cerebellar organization.

claim: In vivo, the receptive fields defined by modulation of PC firing rate could have been misleading since a null net effect could still have masked correlated modifications of excitatory and inhibitory inputs.
source: (2) In vivo, the receptive fields were defined by modulation of the PC firing rate. This parameter could have been misleading since a null net effect could still have masked correlated modifications of excitatory and inhibitory inputs.
evidence: This is speculation about methodological differences between studies.

claim: PF stimulation could induce either LTD at individual sites or LTP at individual sites.
source: We demonstrated that PF stimulation could induce either LTD at individual sites (Hartell, 1996) or LTP at individual sites (Coesmans et al., 2004) indicating that activity-dependent processes can tune GC input maps.
evidence: This is a finding from plasticity experiments supported by citations.

claim: Activity-dependent processes can tune GC input maps.
source: We demonstrated that PF stimulation could induce either LTD at individual sites (Hartell, 1996) or LTP at individual sites (Coesmans et al., 2004) indicating that activity-dependent processes can tune GC input maps.
evidence: This is an inference based on the plasticity experiments.

claim: At the center of the stimulated PF beam, focal synaptic inputs to PC dendrites have likely evoked large calcium transients, similar to CF inputs, and thus induced LTD at these specific GC-PCs synapses.
source: At the center of the stimulated PF beam, focal synaptic inputs to PC dendrites have likely evoked large calcium transients, similar to CF inputs (Hartell, 1996), and thus induced LTD at these specific GC-PCs synapses.
evidence: This is speculation about the mechanism of LTD induction, supported by a citation.

claim: Focal stimulation in the molecular layer may appear non-physiological, but sensory inputs can lead to clustered activation of PFs in vivo.
source: Although focal stimulation in the molecular layer may appear non-physiological, a recent study demonstrated in vivo that sensory inputs can lead to clustered activation of PFs (Wilms and Häusser, 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to justify the experimental approach.

claim: At the periphery of the stimulation beam, sparse activation of PFs might have induced moderate calcium transients leading to LTP.
source: At the periphery of the stimulation beam, sparse activation of PFs might have induced moderate calcium transients leading to LTP (Coesmans et al., 2004).
evidence: This is speculation about the mechanism of LTP induction, supported by a citation.

claim: LTP could favor information transfer between a set of GCs from one microzone and a group of PCs from another microzone.
source: LTP could favor information transfer between a set of GCs from one microzone and a group of PCs from another microzone.
evidence: This is speculation about the functional role of LTP.

claim: LTD, which is physiologically induced by the conjunction of PF and CF inputs to PCs, could limit the communication between microzones.
source: Conversely, LTD, which is physiologically induced by the conjunction of PF and CF inputs to PCs, could limit the communication between these microzones.
evidence: This is speculation about the functional role of LTD based on established knowledge.

claim: Neither the PC clusters nor the GC spatial patterns of connections strictly match with the topography of the spinocerebellar or cuneate MF inputs.
source: Notably, neither the PC clusters nor the GC spatial patterns of connections strictly match with the topography of the spinocerebellar or cuneate MF inputs carrying information from the hindlimb and forelimb
evidence: This is a finding based on comparison of functional and anatomical data.

claim: GC patches might combine MF information from different sources.
source: indicating that GC patches cannot simply be identified by the anatomical organization of a single source of MFs, and might combine MF information from different sources, as suggested in two recent studies (Chabrol et al., 2015; Huang et al., 2013; but see also Bengtsson and Jorntell, 2009).
evidence: This is an inference based on the data and supported by citations.

claim: Discrepancies between anatomical and functional boundaries have been shown using in vivo calcium imaging of CF signaling in PCs following sensory stimulation.
source: Discrepancies between anatomical and functional boundaries have also been shown using in vivo calcium imaging of CF signaling in PCs following sensory stimulation (Tsutsumi et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The functional organization observed might illustrate the importance of connecting cortical microzones controlling similar muscles in both limbs.
source: Since P2+ bands receive specific MF inputs from the hindlimb (Jörntell et al., 2000), the functional organization observed in our experiments might illustrate the importance of connecting cortical microzones controlling similar muscles in both limbs.
evidence: This is speculation about the functional significance of the findings, supported by a citation.

claim: A functional microzone likely computes information from different sources of MF inputs and frequently belongs to two adjacent zebrin bands.
source: Therefore, a functional microzone likely computes information from different sources of MF inputs and frequently belongs to two adjacent zebrin bands as also proposed by (Graham and Wylie, 2012).
evidence: This is an inference based on the data and supported by a citation.

claim: A functional microzonal unit might combine several toolboxes in order to process incoming information.
source: Since zebrin bands also define an array of biochemical markers that can have an important role in synaptic transmission, signal integration and plasticity (for example EAAT4 transporter, PLCbeta3 and 4, IP3R1 and mGluR1a receptors follow a specific zebrin pattern of expression) (Cerminara et al., 2015; Hawkes, 2014; Paukert et al., 2010; Wadiche and Jahr, 2005), a functional microzonal unit might then combine several toolboxes in order to process incoming information.
evidence: This is speculation about functional organization supported by citations.

claim: The area between P2+ ipsi- and contralateral bands could be composed of 10–13 functional units with a mean extension of 70–100 µm.
source: In light of the stereotyped organization of GC input patterns to PCs and MLIs, and the local restriction of the GC inputs to GoCs, we postulate that the area between P2+ ipsi- and contralateral bands could be composed of 10–13 functional units with a mean extension of 70–100 µm, as already suggested by in vivo imaging studies (Ozden et al., 2009; Tsutsumi et al., 2015; Schultz et al., 2009).
evidence: This is speculation based on the data and supported by citations.

claim: In the posterior lobe, zebrin bands and cerebellar inputs have a different topographical organization, notably in the vestibular lobules.
source: In the posterior lobe, zebrin bands and cerebellar inputs have a different topographical organization, notably in the vestibular lobules (Voogd, 2011), but a modular system has also been described suggesting that the communication between microzones through PFs is a general mechanism involved in information processing in the cerebellum.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation.

claim: The communication between microzones through PFs is a general mechanism involved in information processing in the cerebellum.
source: but a modular system has also been described suggesting that the communication between microzones through PFs is a general mechanism involved in information processing in the cerebellum.
evidence: This is speculation about the generality of the findings.

claim: Cortical functional microzones of the cerebellar cortex communicate via the PFs and underlie an important level of coordination between cerebellar modules.
source: In conclusion, we demonstrated that cortical functional microzones of the cerebellar cortex communicate via the PFs and underlie an important level of coordination between cerebellar modules.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the findings.

claim: These properties will favor the synchronization of PCs within specific modules and improve information readout by nuclear cells.
source: These properties will favor the synchronization of PCs within specific modules and improve information readout by nuclear cells (Person and Raman, 2012a; 2012b).
evidence: This is speculation about the functional implications supported by citations.

claim: EAAT4-GFP mice express GFP in zebrin II bands.
source: The use of two distinct specific antibodies against zebrin II/aldolase C (Materials and methods) confirmed that EAAT4-eGFP mice express GFP in zebrin II bands (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from immunohistochemical validation.

claim: Uncaging led to a compound synaptic current in PCs initiated by trains of action potentials in GCs.
source: As uncaging led to a compound synaptic current in PCs initiated by trains of action potentials in GCs (Figure 2B,C; Figure 2—figure supplement 1; Materials and methods)
evidence: This is a finding from the photostimulation experiments.

claim: MFs from the external cuneate and the spinal cord project to the entire depth of the granule cell layer.
source: Since MFs from the external cuneate and the spinal cord project to the entire depth of the granule cell layer (Figure 1C)
evidence: This is a finding from the anatomical tracing experiments.

claim: The average maximum number of evoked action potentials at the center of the photostimulation spot was 19.6 ± 6.6.
source: The average maximum number of evoked action potentials at the center of the spot was 19.6 ± 6.6 (n = 7) indicating that even GC-PC connections with a very low probability of release could evoke a current to the recorded PCs (Isope and Barbour, 2002).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from control experiments.

claim: Each photostimulation beam could illuminate several hundred GCs per 10 µm of slice thickness.
source: We estimated that each beam could illuminate several hundred GCs per 10 µm of slice thickness.
evidence: This is an estimate based on the experimental setup.

claim: Tens of active GC connections could be stimulated simultaneously.
source: Since the synaptic weight of a single GC-PC connection is approximately 0.1 pC (Isope and Barbour, 2002), tens of active GC connections (depending on the depth of the GC layer in the slice) could be stimulated simultaneously, attesting to the efficacy of the photostimulation protocol.
evidence: This is an inference based on the data and cited literature.

claim: The mean deviation of granule cell layer slope from the horizontal axis was 0.85 ± 0.82 deg.
source: A total of 130 axons were traced in 13 slices after the experiment, and the mean deviation from the horizontal axis was 0.85 ± 0.82 deg, suggesting that the absence of distal responses was not due to a tilt in the slice.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from control experiments.

claim: The absence of distal responses was not due to a tilt in the slice.
source: suggesting that the absence of distal responses was not due to a tilt in the slice.
evidence: This is an inference based on the control measurements.
